title: Ventral to Dorsal: Sonic Hedgehog and BMP in the Neural Tube

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: The embryonic {{c1::neural tube}} develops from ectoderm and becomes the brain and spinal cord.
cards.quote: The neural tube is the hollow rod that rolls up from the neural plate, a sheet of ectoderm (the embryo's outer cell layer)

cards.front: What is the notochord, and where does it lie relative to the embryonic neural tube?
cards.back: A rod of mesoderm beneath the neural tube.
cards.quote: The notochord is a rod of mesoderm (the embryo's middle cell layer) running under the tube.

cards.front: Where are the floor plate and roof plate in the embryonic neural tube?
cards.back: The floor plate is the ventral bottom strip just above the notochord; the roof plate is the dorsal top strip.
cards.quote: The floor plate is the tube's bottom strip, a narrow line of specialized cells just above the notochord.

cards.front: Dividing cells in the neural tube ventricular zone that will produce neurons are called {{c1::progenitors}}.
cards.quote: Its cells are progenitors, dividing cells that will make motor neurons near the bottom and relay neurons for body sensation near the top.

cards.front: How do extracellular signals and progenitor cells divide the work of patterning the embryonic spinal cord?
cards.back: Signal sources supply positional gradients; progenitors interpret signal level and duration through transcription factors that sharpen boundaries between identities.
cards.quote: they read the level and how long it lasts, answer with a combination of transcription factors

cards.front: Why does finding two adjacent embryonic tissues with similar properties fail to prove that one induced the other?
cards.back: Similarity could reflect shared developmental history or induction. Moving or removing tissue tests causation more directly than observing adjacency.
cards.quote: That likeness could mean a common history, or it could mean the notochord tells the neural cells what to become.

cards.front: In early chick neural tube assays, a lateral notochord graft induces floor-plate properties, while early notochord removal prevents them. What does each result establish?
cards.back: The graft shows sufficiency for ectopic floor-plate properties; removal shows necessity for normal floor-plate properties in these assays.
cards.quote: The graft shows sufficiency: the notochord is enough to give floor-plate properties in a new place.

cards.front: Recruitment of neighbouring cells to the identity of an already induced tissue is called {{c1::homeogenetic induction}}.
cards.back: Induced floor plate can recruit neural neighbours.
cards.quote: They called this homeogenetic induction: an induced tissue recruits its neighbours to the same identity.

cards.front: Purified Sonic hedgehog signaling fragment induces floor plate at higher concentrations and motor neurons at lower concentrations in neural plate explants. What does this show?
cards.back: One signal can specify different ventral fates at different doses in this assay.
cards.quote: found that higher concentrations induced floor plate and lower ones induced motor neurons.

cards.front: How does Sonic hedgehog change the Patched–Smoothened–Gli pathway in neural progenitors?
cards.back: Shh releases the Patched brake on Smoothened, reducing Gli repressor production and favoring full-length Gli activator.
cards.quote: Shh binds Patched, Patched stops inhibiting Smoothened, and the pathway turns on.
cards.section: How a cell receives it: lifting a brake

cards.front: Which Gli protein is the main repressor, and which acts mainly as the activator in neural tube Shh signaling?
cards.back: Gli3 is the main repressor; Gli2 acts mainly as the activator.
cards.quote: Gli3 is the main repressor; Gli2 is processed poorly and acts mainly as the activator.
cards.section: How a cell receives it: lifting a brake

cards.front: A neural progenitor receives abundant Shh, but cyclopamine is added. What happens to pathway activity and why?
cards.back: Pathway activity switches off: cyclopamine blocks Smoothened, so abundant ligand cannot sustain signaling through it.
cards.quote: blocks Smoothened and so switches the pathway off.
cards.section: How a cell receives it: lifting a brake

cards.front: Loss of developmental gene A removes a cell type. Removing gene B as well restores it. How should the second mutation be classified?
cards.back: It suppresses the first defect: this is a double-mutant rescue and supports a genetic interaction.
cards.quote: If removing a second gene restores what the first loss took away, the second mutation suppresses the first defect.
cards.section: Is Shh needed, and what does it do?

cards.front: Why does rescue of a developmental defect by a second mutation fail, by itself, to establish the molecular mechanism?
cards.back: Rescue establishes a genetic interaction. Other evidence is needed to explain how the genes interact.
cards.quote: It shows the two genes interact, not how; the mechanism needs other evidence.
cards.section: Is Shh needed, and what does it do?

cards.front: Shh-null mice lose most ventral neural tube cell types. Removing Gli3 too restores motor neurons and several ventral interneuron classes. Interpret this using the known pathway.
cards.back: Much of Shh signaling normally counteracts Gli3 repression. Removing that repressor bypasses part of the need for Shh; rescue does not establish complete restoration.
cards.quote: Read with the known pathway, from Patched to Gli, this says that much of what Shh does in the spinal cord is to block Gli3 repressor.
cards.section: Is Shh needed, and what does it do?

cards.front: A signal that spreads from a source and specifies different identities at different concentrations is a {{c1::morphogen}}.
cards.quote: A morphogen is a signal that spreads from a source and gives different instructions at different concentrations.
cards.section: Reading the slope: a code written in two classes

cards.front: How do class I and class II transcription factors respond differently to Shh in ventral neural progenitors?
cards.back: Shh represses class I factors, such as Pax6, and induces class II factors, such as Nkx2.2; staggered expression borders create distinct factor combinations.
cards.quote: Because the borders are staggered, every stretch of the wall between two borders carries a different combination of factors.
cards.section: Reading the slope: a code written in two classes

cards.front: Which three markers serve as landmarks for the dorsal half, motor-neuron progenitors, and the domain beside the floor plate?
cards.back: Pax7: dorsal half; Olig2: motor-neuron progenitors; Nkx2.2: domain beside the floor plate. These landmarks do not distinguish every domain.
cards.quote: Pax7 for the dorsal half, Olig2 for motor-neuron progenitors and Nkx2.2 for the domain beside the floor plate.
cards.section: Reading the slope: a code written in two classes

cards.front: From ventral to dorsal, what is the order of neuronal outputs from spinal progenitor domains p3, pMN, p2, p1 and p0?
cards.back: V3 interneurons → motor neurons → V2 interneurons → V1 interneurons → V0 interneurons.
cards.quote: The ventral half of the wall will hold five stripes of progenitors, called domains, each making one class of neuron.

cards.front: In the simplified spinal progenitor code, sample A expresses Olig2 and low Pax6; sample B lacks Olig2 but expresses Irx3, full-level Pax6 and Nkx6.1. Identify their domains.
cards.back: A is pMN; B is p2. Nkx6.1 distinguishes B from p0 and p1, which also express Irx3 and full-level Pax6 without Olig2.
cards.quote: Compared with pMN, p2 lacks Olig2 and has Irx3, with Pax6 back at full level.
cards.section: Reading the slope: a code written in two classes

cards.front: Why does inducing more Patched1 provide negative feedback during Shh signaling in chick neural progenitors?
cards.back: Patched is a brake; increasing it raises the Shh needed to sustain signaling, contributing to adaptation.
cards.why: Patched1 also binds Shh and limits its spread, so responding cells help shape the gradient they read.
cards.quote: In chick neural cells, that extra brake contributes to adaptation: it then takes more Shh to keep signaling.

cards.front: Two chick neural cell cultures start signaling together at low or high Shh doses. Both accumulate the Patched1 brake. Which should fall below its signaling threshold first, and why?
cards.back: The low-dose culture should fall below threshold first, because less Shh is available to overcome the growing Patched1 brake.
cards.quote: The low-dose cell, because less Shh is left to overcome the rising brake.

cards.front: Neural progenitor cultures receive the same signal concentration for different durations and are scored at the same developmental age. Longer exposure gives more ventral identities. What does this establish?
cards.back: Exposure duration carries identity information independently of concentration in this comparison; dose alone cannot explain the different outcomes.
cards.quote: held the dose fixed in chick explants and varied exposure time, and longer exposure gave progressively more ventral identities.

cards.front: Matched chick neural explants receive Shh initially. Signaling is then blocked in one group and maintained in the other. The blocked group becomes more dorsal. What does this show?
cards.back: Ventral identity still needs signaling for a period after induction; an initial exposure does not make it permanently independent of Shh.
cards.quote: ending Shh signaling with cyclopamine after a period of exposure let cells fall back to more dorsal identities than continued exposure gave

cards.front: In the illustrative stationary-cell model, a Hill-1 response spans an 81-fold Shh change from 10% to 90%. Shh falls e-fold every 20 micrometres; cells are 5 micrometres wide. Estimate the transition width in cells.
cards.back: Width = 20 × ln(81) = 87.9 micrometres; 87.9/5 = 17.6, about 18 cells. These are illustrative model values, not a measured border width.
cards.quote: An 81-fold change is 4.4 such steps (the natural log of 81), so it spans about 90 micrometres, roughly 18 cells of in-between answers.

cards.front: How can mutual repression between transcription factors turn a smooth developmental signal gradient into sharp cell-identity boundaries?
cards.back: Strong mutual repression pushes cells toward one factor program or the other, reducing intermediate identities and helping maintain distinct neighbouring domains.
cards.quote: In a strongly cross-repressive circuit a cell near a border is pushed toward one state or the other and cannot hold both for long.

cards.front: In simple models of mutually repressive developmental factors, what distinguishes a bistable switch from a weak repression loop?
cards.back: Strong, cooperative repression can support two stable states; a weak loop has one steady state and no switch.
cards.quote: In simple models they do so only when the repression is strong and cooperative; a weak loop has a single steady state and no switch.

cards.front: Irx3 is experimentally maintained in pMN progenitors despite their normal Olig2 program. What happens to Olig2 and motor-neuron identity, based on the cross-repression rule?
cards.back: Olig2 should fall and motor-neuron identity should be weakened, because Irx3 represses Olig2. This prediction alone does not specify a complete replacement fate.
cards.quote: Irx3 and Olig2 repress each other at the dorsal edge of pMN.

cards.front: In cultured mouse embryos, a short Smoothened-activating drug pulse leaves progenitor borders nearly normal, while continuous treatment shifts them. What property of the network does this support?
cards.back: Some memory or buffering of brief signal changes, with susceptibility to sustained input. The pulse result does not imply that borders can never move.
cards.quote: a short pulse of a drug that activates Smoothened left the borders close to their normal positions; continuous treatment shifted them.

cards.front: Why can a sharply defined developmental boundary still be in the wrong position?
cards.back: Cross-repression sharpens the identity decision, but a sustained signal-reading error can select and stabilize the wrong identity.
cards.quote: Cross-repression makes a border sharp, not necessarily accurately placed.

cards.front: A progenitor network has strong mutual repression. A sustained error in morphogen reading shifts a boundary, then the reading becomes normal. Must the boundary immediately return, and why?
cards.back: No. The rules that cross-repression gives memory and can hold a signal-reading error allow a misplaced boundary to persist. Whether it returns depends on subsequent signaling; sharpness alone does not guarantee accuracy.
cards.quote: A large or lasting misreading of the Shh level can tip a cell to the wrong side, and the switch may then hold the error;

cards.front: How are the dorsal neural tube signaling sources established, and which signals does the roof plate supply?
cards.back: Epidermal BMPs are proposed to induce the roof plate, which supplies related BMP signals and also Wnts, including Wnt1 and Wnt3a.
cards.quote: BMPs from the epidermis induce the roof plate, which becomes a second source of related signals.
cards.section: The top of the tube: BMPs from the epidermis and roof plate

cards.front: From top to bottom, the dorsal spinal neural tube produces six early interneuron classes named {{c1::dI1 to dI6}}.
cards.quote: The dorsal tube makes six early classes of interneurons, named dI1 to dI6 from the top down.
cards.section: The top of the tube: BMPs from the epidermis and roof plate

cards.front: After early roof-plate ablation in mice, dI1–dI3 fail to form but dI4–dI6 do not show the same dependence. What does this establish about dorsal patterning?
cards.back: The roof plate is needed for the three dorsal-most classes in this experiment; its necessity cannot be generalized to all six dorsal classes.
cards.quote: The classes nearest the roof plate needed it; dI4 to dI6, further away, did not depend on it in that experiment
cards.section: The top of the tube: BMPs from the epidermis and roof plate

cards.front: In illustrative chick explant data at 4 nM Shh, adding BMP7 lowers Nkx2.2-positive explants from 80% to 20%. Calculate the percentage-point decrease and relative reduction, then interpret the direction.
cards.back: Decrease = 80 − 20 = 60 percentage points. Relative reduction = (80 − 20)/80 × 100 = 75%. This supports BMP7 opposing the Shh response under these conditions.
cards.quote: The two systems also oppose each other: BMP signaling alters the response to Shh
cards.section: The top of the tube: BMPs from the epidermis and roof plate

cards.front: Design two chick neural plate explant series to distinguish effects of Shh concentration from effects of exposure duration. How should the scoring time be controlled?
cards.back: Vary dose at fixed duration, then duration at fixed dose; score at one developmental age. In these chick explant assays, higher doses at fixed duration and longer exposure at fixed dose give more ventral identities.
cards.quote: At a fixed time, higher doses push cells ventrally; at a fixed dose, longer exposure does too.

cards.front: A developmental marker is absent at the final endpoint after signal withdrawal. How would you distinguish failed induction from loss of an initially induced identity?
cards.back: Also score the marker at withdrawal, or score neuronal outputs. A positive marker at withdrawal followed by absence later supports loss. This uses the rules that signaling induces identity and may also be needed to maintain it.
cards.quote: Because progenitors can lose these markers once signaling stops, also score them at the time cyclopamine goes on, or score the neurons they made.

cards.front: Shh dose assays suggest a ventral fate ladder, but mouse floor plate needs Gli2 while motor neurons form without it. What limit does this place on treating floor plate as simply a higher-dose motor-neuron fate?
cards.back: The dose ladder alone is insufficient. The stated rules give floor plate a distinct Gli2 requirement and an early high-signal requirement, so fate depends on pathway components and timing as well as concentration.
cards.quote: In the mouse, floor plate needs Gli2 and an early period of high signaling, while motor neurons form without Gli2
cards.section: Where the floor plate comes from

cards.front: In mice lacking Pax6 and Olig2, Nkx2.2 expands dorsally but the measured Gli-reporter domain does not. How does this constrain an explanation based only on a changed Shh gradient?
cards.back: A changed gradient alone is insufficient to explain the observations: the rule that transcription-factor interactions interpret input permits a fate boundary to move without a matching reporter shift. The reporter does not measure every feature of signaling.
cards.quote: losing the network moved the border, without a matching shift in the reporter.

cards.front: A progenitor averages repeated readings of a morphogen before choosing an identity. Compare independent random reading errors with a bias shared by every reading. Which can averaging reduce, and what does this mean for boundary placement?
cards.back: Averaging can reduce independent error, but shared bias remains and can still misplace the boundary. This combines the stated averaging rule with the rule that a sharp identity switch does not guarantee accurate placement.
cards.quote: averaging does not remove an error shared by every reading.
